input: I hold my hand where Professor Stone can inspect the signet, keeping the ring on my finger. "Of course. The lawyers could tell me whose it was, but very little about the man." I notice his lowered voice and keep mine quiet too. "What was Dan Garvey like? If this isn't the place for that conversation, I'd be glad to find another time."
output:
Stone bends close, careful not to touch. The hall’s white lamps catch the worn sheaf and the nick beside it.

“Yes. Same ring.” His thumb rubs unconsciously against his own bare forefinger. “He made that mark on a map case. The latch stuck; Dan decided this was a constitutional dispute between himself and the furniture.”

Ashworth’s mouth creases. “Who prevailed?”

“The furniture, briefly.” Stone straightens. “I catalogued documents for him when I was seventeen. He remembered every clerk’s name, made indefensible tea, and read footnotes before summaries. If someone called a matter simple, he became suspicious.”

Professor Windwhisper approaches with soundless steps, silver hair bright beneath the lamps. “A useful habit, when moderated.”

Stone’s shoulders draw in by a degree. “The library, tomorrow at eighth bell, if you wish. I can tell you the ordinary things about him.” After the smallest pause: “Those matter too.”

“Family recollections are valuable,” Windwhisper says. “Provided recollection and record remain distinct.”

The reception bell rings before Stone can answer. Ashworth lays a light hand between Stone’s shoulders and steers both of you toward the banners.

“Duty calls. Rowan, you must stand beneath the newly ironed symbol of your people while strangers congratulate you on events for which you bear no responsibility.”

The first delegations begin to advance. Before they reach you, a red-luminous woman slips sideways out of the crowd carrying two glasses. Elven points rise through her dark hair; small horns curve above them, and a gold slit-pupiled gaze measures you with frank amusement.

“Lysara Vane,” she says. “Exceptional-case observer. The chancellor’s speech places us in adjacent paragraphs, so I thought we should meet before becoming a rhetorical device.”

She offers you one glass.

“It’s only water. They don’t trust history-making admissions with wine until after the formal congratulations.”
